title: A24 on Top: With Bigger Budgets, Better Box Office and Splashy IP, Is it Finally Time to Sell?
description: “Elden Ring,” one of the most popular video games of all time, takes place in a fantasy realm called the Lands Between — a space between life and de
body:
“Elden Ring,” one of the most popular video games of all time, takes place in a fantasy realm called the Lands Between — a space between life and death where humans battle gods and monsters for power.

	A24 has just wrapped production on the movie adaptation, representing the company’s biggest swing to date. The action epic, starring Kit Connor and directed by Alex Garland, carries an enormous $200 million price tag. The film’s otherworldly setting is fitting, as the art-house giant currently occupies a land between: no longer a scrappy indie studio challenging the establishment, not yet a merged or acquired corporate monolith scaling up to the major studio table.
	

	But this year will go down as A24’s most profitable ever thanks to the runaway success of Gen Z horror breakout “Backrooms” and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s lightning rod Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything.” Those titles and others have boosted A24 above $500 million at the domestic box office for the first time.

	A24 may also eke out bragging rights as the most nominated studio at the Oscars, just as its fledgling TV division has started producing serious hits (following up HBO’s “Euphoria” with Peacock’s “Crystal Lake,” HBO’s “Neighbors” and Apple TV’s “Margot’s Got Money Troubles”). The traction that A24 is enjoying in this moment of massive disruption and consolidation across the industry is a true flex from one of entertainment’s most bulletproof brands. But all of this momentum raises the question: What does A24 want to be?
	

	“If they’re ever going to monetize, this is the time to do it,” one high-flying mogul says of A24. Speculation about the studio’s M&A potential has been floating around town since its 2013 inception. Led by founders David Fenkel and Daniel Katz, A24 has over the years flirted with buyers like Apple and Sony. But no deal has materialized because Fenkel and Katz have ruthlessly protected A24’s cool factor (the abstract secret sauce that’s trained younger generations to reclaim the moviegoing experience and make edgy auteurs their idols). They’ve turned down a host of recent offers for equity investments and held creative control as tightly as first-person gamers treasure the mythical forces of “Elden Ring.” 

	Inside A24, the reigning logic for the past several years has been “grow from within,” as underscored by the 2021 hire of NBA chief financial officer J.B. Lockhart to help the company scale at a cautious pace. Insiders also credit chief operating officer Matt Bires (an architect of A24’s Cherry Lane Theater acquisition), global TV head Ravi Nandan (the Fielder whisperer) and the all-important chief marketer Graham Retzlik with the steady growth. But make no mistake, the source says, “Fenkel and Katz are absolutely interested in getting rich.”

	A24’s last fundraise came in mid-2024, courtesy of Josh Kushner’s Thrive Capital, and valued the company at $3.5 billion. It’s a modest sum compared with the eye-popping $111 billion check that Skydance wrote to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, but nevertheless a number that three sources at rival companies find out of line with market realities. 

	“They’ve got a great brand, but in an acquisition scenario, we’ve seen that brands don’t really survive. Look at what Disney did to FX and 20th Century Fox,” says another top executive. “Their earnings look good, especially this year, but the pressure is on to grow into the valuation they chased.”

	To that end, the studio has been experimenting with bigger price tags and splashier IP, like a massive recent deal for the film and TV rights to “The Texas Chainsaw Massacre.” However, the studio’s efforts to scale beyond its low-budget roots have been mixed. Dice rolls last year — like Ari Aster’s “Eddington” and Dwayne Johnson’s “The Smashing Machine,” each of which cost $50 million — were rejected at the box office.
	

	Despite the rough 2025 returns, A24 rebounded this year in a big way. “You Can See Everything” (a staggering $64 million to date) and “The Drama,” an offbeat relationship comedy starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson ($134 million globally), became breakout hits in genres that don’t always resonate on the big screen. That’s to say nothing of “Backrooms,” a wildly profitable sensation that became the studio’s highest grossing film ever with $400 million globally against a $10 million budget. Over the summer, A24 managed to beat Warner Bros. and Paramount in terms of market share, one of the rare moments an indie has outgrossed the major studios during what’s usually the busiest time for moviegoing. All the riches on “Backrooms” and “You Can See Everything” will mop up the red ink from misses such as Glen Powell’s action comedy “How to Make a Killing” ($21 million against a $15 million budget), Hugh Jackman’s revisionist “The Death of Robin Hood” ($9.8 million against a $20 million budget) and Chris Rock’s dramedy “Misty Green” ($160,000 against a $5 million budget).

	Rivals gripe that A24 is savvy about burying its failures. That’s partially because the company doesn’t handle the overseas rollout of its films, instead selling the foreign rights to regional distributors. That helps the studio recoup losses for underperforming movies. Yet it also means A24 doesn’t get to enjoy the outsize riches when a title like “Backrooms” earns more than $200 million internationally. 

	According to a recent Wall Street Journal story, Fenkel and Katz have been flying around the globe for the past year to look for “potential partners” to help A24 establish ports in foreign markets. The reported plan is finding local language teams with similar sensibilities as the U.S. outfit. Placing that kind of creative trust in satellite offices could be a risky proposition, though less expensive than building out an international distribution engine. The founders don’t seem to mind racking up sky miles — A24 was, perhaps preciously, named after the highway that connects Rome to the quaint Italian mountain town of Teroma.

	As A24 scales up with bigger budgets, a challenge will be connecting with audiences beyond the coasts. Part of the charm to cinephiles and allure for auteurs is that the studio isn’t trying to make movies for everyone. Some of the company’s buzziest films were wildly polarizing. Consider the CinemaScore for favorites like favorites like “Hereditary” (D+), Adam Sandler’s “Uncut Gems” (C+) or “Backrooms” (B-). None of those movies cost above $20 million to produce, so they didn’t need to resonate with the masses. However, “Elden Ring” and next year’s $35 million slasher “Slayground” can’t afford to alienate most of the country.
	

	“When you get into these price tags, you have to talk four quadrants. A24 didn’t build their brand on four-quadrant films. They chased two quadrants very hard,” says Travis Knox, associate professor of producing at Chapman University. “At $100 million-plus budgets, you can’t ignore Oklahoma and Indiana.”

	Beyond the movies, TV shows and viral merchandise, A24 has physical assets in New York’s Cherry Lane Theatre and a controversial $75 million investment from Google DeepMind to develop AI tools for filmmakers. Those are value adds for a big-ticket sale, though Knox points to an important caveat for any deal. The single greatest asset that A24 has is the power of its brand to bring younger audiences to theaters and TV platforms without the stench of corporate greed.

	“If they were purchased by, say, Amazon … it would automatically alienate the audience,” says Knox.

schema.headline: A24 on Top: With Bigger Budgets, Better Box Office and Splashy IP, Is it Finally Time to Sell?

title: UFC’s Event Sellout Spree Powers TKO Q3 Earnings
description: UFC had the wind at its back in the third quarter with a string of sellout events that pushed revenue and adjusted earnings for the league’s parent
body:
UFC had the wind at its back in the third quarter with a string of sellout events that pushed revenue and adjusted earnings for the league’s parent company, TKO, to new heights. 

	UFC delivered double-digit gains in the quarter across all key measures. Revenue climbed 60% year-over-year to $519.2 million, thanks to a $132.3 million increase in media rights, production and content revenue. Live events and hospitality revenue spiked by $36 million, in addition to a $20.5 million increase in partnerships and marketing revenue and a $5.2 million boost in consumer products licensing and other revenue.
	

	WWE, on the other hand, had a tougher quarter in part because there were three more events on the wrestling league’s main roster in the comparable year-ago quarter. Nevertheless, the full-year forecast for both UFC, WWE and IMG, which includes the On Location premium events business, which also had a strong quarter thanks to the influx of big-ticket events around the World Cup.

	“Our third quarter performance reflects the secular tail winds powering live events and experiences around the world, and TKO’s assets sit front and center of that premium ecosystem,” said Mark Shapiro, president and COO of TKO. “As we close out what we’ve called our year of execution, our decision to raise full-year guidance for the second time this year is the clearest expression of our conviction across the entire portfolio. Our business is durable and our fundamentals are solid, with the vast majority of our existing revenues locked in for the next five to seven years. Macro trends are firmly in our favor, every facet of sports consumption is pointing north, and we see substantial runway ahead.”
	

	For the quarter, TKO delivered total revenue of $1.36 billion, up 21%. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, spiked 54%, to $555.7 million, powered by an increase of$119.7 million at UFC and a gain of $9.4 million at WWE. Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded nicely to 41%, up from 32% a year ago. With these trends, TKO has increased its full-year revenue and adjusted earnings target for the full year $5.790 billion to $5.830 billion for revenue and $2.295 billion to $2.315 billion for adjusted EBITDA.

	More to come

title: ‘Dune 3’ Cast Says the Movie Takes ‘Departures’ From the Books, but ‘You’re Crazy If You’re Going to Pick Fault’ With It
description: The cast of Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune 3” is getting the word out early: There will be major “departures” form Frank Herbert’s literary franchise in
body:
The cast of Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune 3” is getting the word out early: There will be major “departures” form Frank Herbert’s literary franchise in the upcoming film, which is set to pull heavily from Herbert’s 1969 sequel novel “Dune Messiah.”

	“There’s a lot in this film that is very true to the source material, and there are departures,” Zendaya told The New York Times, with franchise newcomer Robert Pattinson adding: “You got to be kind of crazy if you’re going to be picking fault with this one [over the changes to the books].”
	

	“The script was really cool, but it was quite complicated,” added Pattinson, who makes his “Dune” debut as Scytale. “And watching the film, it’s not about what I thought it was going to be about at all. It reads as much more of a grand political, moral fable, and the movie is so much more emotional. A lot of it is about parenting, and I just thought it was so moving.”

	When asked if he was satisfied with Villeneuve’s ending of the film trilogy, franchise star Timothée Chalamet answered: “Absolutely. It didn’t feel like the bar dropped at all, Denis just changed the location of the bar. This movie is its own thing.”

	“Dune 3” arrives in theaters at the tail end of a successful year at the box office. It’s opening weekend alongside “Avengers: Doomsday” is widely expected to be the highest-grossing single weekend in box office history. Florence Pugh, who returns in the third movie as Irulan, credits the “Dune” movies with bringing “back moviegoing” following the pandemic and various Hollywood strikes. The first “Dune” movie opened simultaneously in theaters and on HBO Max and grossed $410 million worldwide, no small feat in 2021 when Hollywood was still being disrupted by COVID. The 2024 sequel received an exclusive theatrical release and earned a mighty $714 million.
	

	“What an event the second one was,” Pugh told The Times. “It was just so lovely to be a part of something that we know is our generational kind of ‘Star Wars.'”

	Zendaya added, “Any opportunity that we have that we can hopefully contribute to the moviegoing experience and keep that alive, because it’s so much a part of my life, my childhood, so many people’s lives — it’s the reason we do it.”

	“Dune 3” opens in theaters Dec. 18 from Warner Bros and Legendary.

schema.headline: ‘Dune 3’ Cast Says the Movie Takes ‘Departures’ From the Books, but ‘You’re Crazy If You’re Going to Pick Fault’ With It

title: Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ to Lead With $30 Million Opening Weekend, ‘Cat in the Hat’ Aims for $20 Million Debut
description: “Godzilla Minus Zero” should stomp to the top of box office charts, with the Kaiju sequel on track to earn a strong $30 million from 3,254 North Am
body:
“Godzilla Minus Zero” should stomp to the top of box office charts, with the Kaiju sequel on track to earn a strong $30 million from 3,254 North American theaters in its opening weekend.

	The action adventure will tower over fellow newcomers including Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat” and Searchlight’s dark buddy comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and directed by Martin McDonagh. “The Cat in the Hat” is aiming for second place with $20 million to $25 million from 4,000 domestic venues. “Wild Horse Nine” is targeting $5 million to $7 million from just 1,000 screens.
	

	“Godzilla Minus Zero” will build on the excitement from 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” a sci-fi epic that surprised in the U.S. with $11.4 million domestically to start. With great reviews and a lack of competition (it debuted during Hollywood’s actors and writers strike), “Godzilla Minus One” powered to $57 million to stand as the highest-grossing live-action Japanese film in North America. Globally, the film earned $113 million and won a visual effects Oscar.

	Produced by Japan’s Toho and distributed in the U.S. by GKids, “Godzilla Minus Zero” should overindex on premium large formats; it’s the first Japanese production ever filmed for Imax. Directed by Takashi Yamazaki, the movie takes place two years after the prior installment as Godzilla regenerates and resurfaces to combat a new monster that’s tormenting postwar Japan. Reviews have been overwhelmingly positive, with Variety’s chief film critic Owen Gleiberman calling the sequel an “even grander follow-up to ‘Godzilla Minus One.'”
	

	“Cat in the Hat” is tracking a much lower opening than prior animated Dr. Seuss adaptations. By comparison, 2018’s “The Grinch” opened to $67 million, and 2012’s “The Lorax” opened to $70 million, neither adjusted for inflation. Sure, the theatrical landscape has changed dramatically since those films were released. However this spring’s “Hoppers,” an original offering from Pixar, managed to debut to $45 million. Recently, though, animated movies based on popular IP have enjoyed long theatrical lives, and the studio is hoping “Cat in the Hat” performs similarly to Sony’s 2024 adventure “Garfield,” which bowed to $23 million and powered to $91 million domestically and $257 million globally. 

	“Cat in the Hat” will rely on word-of-mouth, as well as overseas audiences, to achieve the staying power necessary to justify its $92 million production budget. (Theater owners keep roughly 50% of ticket sales.) The movie could benefit because there hasn’t been an animated offering for families with young kids since September’s “Forgotten Island.” And “Cat in the Hat” won’t have direct competition until Disney’s original “Hexed” launches on Nov. 25.

	This is the second adaptation of the Seuss classic following 2003’s live-action comedy, starring Mike Myers as the Cat. That film opened to $38 million, not adjusted for inflation, and ran out of steam with $134 million, a disappointing result given the budget was above $100 million. Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartooned version, which was directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja and revolves around the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous cat (wearing a hat) arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town.

	“Wild Horse Nine” is catering to older audiences, a demographic that’s been hit or miss in recent years. Searchlight is opting to launch the movie in roughly 1,000 theaters, a larger initial footprint compared to McDonagh’s prior film, 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin.” After a start in limited release, “Banshees of Inisherin” became a slow and steady box office winner with $10.5 million domestically and $50 million globally. “Wild Horse Nine,” which similarly hopes to find itself in the Oscar race, follows two CIA officers (Malkovich and Rockwell) who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island shortly before a Chilean military coup.
	

	This weekend’s other newcomer is the Indian epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” which is projected to earn $6 million during its first four days in theaters. Those ticket sales are comparable to recent Telugu language fantasy films like “Kalki 2898 AD” ($5.6 million), “Devara Part 1” ($5.6 million) and “Pushpa: The Rule – Part 2” ($5 million) — all of which were released in 2024 and legged out to various degrees. Sony is distributing “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” in 1,300 theaters, marking the widest North American release for an Indian film.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ to Lead With $30 Million Opening Weekend, ‘Cat in the Hat’ Aims for $20 Million Debut

title: Tony Awards Will Remain on CBS Through 2032 Under New Five-Year Deal
description: The Tony Awards will remain on CBS under a new five-year deal announced Wednesday. The network revealed that it has sealed a new broadcast agreemen
body:
The Tony Awards will remain on CBS under a new five-year deal announced Wednesday. The network revealed that it has sealed a new broadcast agreement with the American Theatre Wing and The Broadway League that will keep the kudocast on CBS through 2032. 

	The Tonys have been on CBS since 1978 — and now reps the longest-running major awards show/network partnership, as the Grammys, Oscars, Golden Globes and Emmys have all struck new deals in recent years, moving from their longtime homes. 
	

	The deal also means the 80th annual Tony Awards, broadcast from New York’s Radio City Music Hall, will air live on CBS (and the premium tier of Paramount+) on June 13, 2027, at 8 p.m. ET / 5 p.m. PT.

	“CBS has a celebrated history of supporting the creative arts on television and the Tony Awards are a cornerstone of that past, present and future,” said CBS Entertainment president Amy Reisenbach in a statement. “George Cheeks and I are thrilled to extend the Network’s 48-year partnership with the American Theatre Wing and The Broadway League and showcase the extraordinary talent, unforgettable performances and incomparable energy of Broadway to viewers across the country for years to come.”

	Tony Awards Prods., a joint venture of the American Theatre Wing and The Broadway League, produces the Tonys. Raj Kapoor, Sarah Levine Hall and Jack Sussman are set to produce the 2027 show. Kapoor and Levine Hall are co-showrunners, while Patrick Menton and Rob Paine are co-executive producers. Menton also serves as head of talent.

	“We are thrilled to extend our long-standing partnership with CBS. For the past 48 years, we have collaborated with CBS to bring the best of Broadway to theater fans all around the world and we look forward to marking the 80th anniversary of the Tony Awards with our best show yet,” said Heather Hitchens, president and CEO of the American Theatre Wing, and Jason Laks, president of The Broadway League, in a joint statement.

schema.headline: Tony Awards Will Remain on CBS Through 2032 Under New Five-Year Deal

title: ‘Club Kid,’ ‘Queen at Sea’ Earn Top Prizes at Philadelphia Film Festival; 35th Edition Sets All-Time Attendance Record (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Lance Hammer’s “Queen at Sea” and Jordan Firstman‘s “Club Kid” earned top honors at the Philadelphia Film Festival, taking home the narrative jury
body:
Lance Hammer’s “Queen at Sea” and Jordan Firstman‘s “Club Kid” earned top honors at the Philadelphia Film Festival, taking home the narrative jury prize and the narrative audience award, respectively. This year’s festival, which marked the 35th edition, drew the highest attendance in PFF history. 

	In his recent cover story with Variety, Firstman shared his excitement that “Club Kid,” despite centering on the granular world of New York’s queer clubbing scene, touched a diverse range of movie fans as an intimate family drama about a long-lost son and a young father coming into his own. 
	

	“It’s been amazing to see the kinds of people that relate to this film, but it really is a movie about growth,” Firstman said. “In Telluride, I watched a 75-year-old conservative man leave the theater in tears. Then we took it to the New York Film Festival, which I was very nervous to do, and showed it to the 35-year-olds who do drugs. I built the story to work on levels, with the top being a layer of warmth that feels like a hug. I explore some of my more transgressive ideas beneath the surface. If you don’t get it, there’s still a story that will make you laugh and feel something.”

	Other PFF honorees included Liese’s “Seized,” which won the jury award for best documentary feature. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s devastating Gaza doc “Naza” and David Greaves, Liani Greaves and William Greaves’ intimate look-back at the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” shared the documentary audience prize. “Big Phan,” a biopic about the Phillie Phanatic, earned the audience award for local feature. 
	

	Philadelphia-area filmmaking award winners were “The Haunting of Pennhurst,” from directors Mike Attie, Katarina Poljak and Nathan Stenberg, which won best Filmadelphia feature. Dana Nachman’s “The Second Life of Freddie Nole” took home best Filmadelphia short.

	Rounding out the jury categories was Stephen P. Neary’s “Living with a Visionary,” which won best short film. PFF also honored actor and filmmaker Tim Blake Nelson with the artistic achievement in directing award for his new feature, “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd.”

	See a full list of audience and jury award winners below.

NearyHonorable Mention: Jimmy’s Custom Coffin — Director: James P. title: Inde Navarrette’s ‘SNL’ Episode Hits Season High of 5.2 Million Viewers
description: Inde Navarrette‘s hot streak isn’t ending anytime soon. The “Obsession” star brought “Saturday Night Live” its biggest audience of the season thus
body:
Inde Navarrette‘s hot streak isn’t ending anytime soon. The “Obsession” star brought “Saturday Night Live” its biggest audience of the season thus far as the host of the Halloween episode, which hit 5.2 million viewers.

	Not only does that put Navarrette above Season 52’s previous hosts — Knicks superstar Jalen Brunson, Dakota Johnson (featuring a cameo from Taylor Swift) and a controversial Shane Gillis — but it’s an impressive showing compared with some of the biggest episodes in recent “SNL” history. During Season 51, only two episodes surpassed 5.2 million viewers, and both featured major stars: Bowen Yang’s final episode as a cast member, which was hosted by Ariana Grande in December 2025 with Cher as musical guest (5.4 million viewers), and the season finale, which was hosted by “SNL” alum Will Ferrell and featured Paul McCartney as musical guest (5.3 million viewers).
	

	Navarrette’s “SNL” episode also had the best performance on Peacock specifically since the Season 51 episode in March that featured Harry Styles as host and musical guest. And among adults age 18-49, it scored the show’s best rating since the November 2024 episode hosted by John Mulaney. Video content from the episode garnered 325 million video views across YouTube, Facebook, X, Instagram and TikTok — a season high.

	Navarrette was joined by musical guest Gracie Abrams. The episode also featured Tom Hanks reprising his David S. Pumpkins sketch alongside “SNL” alum Bobby Moynihan.

	Up next on Nov. 7, “SNL” will be hosted by Druski with the Strokes as musical guest. On Nov. 14, Mulaney will have his seventh hosting stint alongside Phoebe Bridgers.

schema.headline: Inde Navarrette’s ‘SNL’ Episode Hits Season High of 5.2 Million Viewers

title: Maya Hawke to Star in ‘Magic: The Gathering’ Movie
description:
Maya Hawke will star in “Magic: The Gathering,” a movie version of the wildly popular trading card game.

	Hawke’s role has not been disclosed. Plo
body:
Maya Hawke will star in “Magic: The Gathering,” a movie version of the wildly popular trading card game.

	Hawke’s role has not been disclosed. Plot details also remain under wraps, though the tabletop game is set across a multiverse of fantasy worlds and involves players who are engaged in a battle, acting as wizards known as Planeswalkers. Hawke is expected to anchor a yet-to-be-cast ensemble of actors, according to Deadline, which first reported the news.
	

	Legendary Entertainment and Hasbro Entertainment are producing the live-action movie, with Matt Johnson (“Blackberry,” “Nirvanna the Band the Show”) set to direct. Johnson, a longtime “Magic: The Gathering” fan, is also writing the screenplay with Noah Gardner (“Super 8”) and Aidan Fitzgerald (“Calls”). 

	“I was x&0 with good breakers going into day 2 of GP Detroit and telling myself, ‘I’m going to drop out of film school and become a pro Magic player,’” Johnson said. “Pod one I’m seated across from Rich Hoaen. By round five I’m x&5 and tilted so badly that I sac Lifespinner and a lethal board (I’m serious) for a lone Jugan. My opponent goes end-step Rend Spirit and within 10 minutes I’m driving back to Toronto thinking ‘My Magic career is officially over.’ To all the dreamers reading this: in every pool, there is a day 2 deck.”

	Hawke is best known for Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” and she’s also appeared in projects like Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Wes Anderson’s “Asteroid City,” Jennifer Kaytin Robinson’s feature “Do Revenge,” and Bradley Cooper’s “Maestro.” She voiced Anxiety in Pixar’s “Inside Out 2.” She’s next starring in Lionsgate’s “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

schema.headline: Maya Hawke to Star in ‘Magic: The Gathering’ Movie

title: Matt Friend Signs With Range Media Partners (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Matt Friend has signed with Range Media Partners for representation.

	The 28-year-old comedian has gone viral on social media for his arsenal of i
body:
Matt Friend has signed with Range Media Partners for representation.

	The 28-year-old comedian has gone viral on social media for his arsenal of impressions, which includes 250 distinct voices from Donald Trump to Rami Malek. 

	Friend has made a name for himself performing impressions in front of the subjects themselves. He’s done Barack Obama with the former president, he’s accosted Andy Cohen and Will Arnett on the street and he’s imitated the host of “The Howard Stern Show” while sitting on its famous couch. He has amassed over 5 million followers across social media platforms.
	

	Friend has also become a fixture of many red carpets including the Golden Globes and Netflix’s “Roast of Kevin Hart.” And his appearances include “The Drew Barrymore Show,” “Good Morning America,” “The Today Show,” “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and MSNBC, CNN and Fox News, where he tickles the conservative hosts with his Trump impression. In 2024, he appeared at the White House Correspondents Dinner, where he did Trump for then-President Joe Biden.

	He has anchored events like the Snappy Awards and NHL Awards, and he hosted a CNN special called “America Laughs With Matt Friend,” which had a political bent. In October, he debuted a comedy segment on Prime Video’s “Thursday Night Football.” 

	On television, Friend’s voice credits include “The Simpsons” and “Family Guy.” (He played a version of Jeff Goldblum on both animated series.) He will also be heard in the upcoming “CoComelon: The Movie,” due 2027.

	Friend continues to be represented by CAA, Sunshine Sachs Morgan & Lylis, and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller.

schema.headline: Matt Friend Signs With Range Media Partners (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Variety’s 10 Comics to Watch for 2026
description:
Nov 4, 2026 12:00pm PT	
	


	Adam Friedland, Kyle Gordon, Wally Baram, Usama Siddiquee and more honorees will perform at a New York
body:
Nov 4, 2026 12:00pm PT	
	


	Adam Friedland, Kyle Gordon, Wally Baram, Usama Siddiquee and more honorees will perform at a New York Comedy Festival showcase on Nov. 12.
	
			


			
			
	

	

		
	
				

	Since the turn of the century, Variety has scoped out the next generation of comedy stars through our annual 10 Comics to Watch franchise. The inaugural lineup in 2000 included future industry favorites Zach Galifianakis, Maria Bamford, Patton Oswalt and Louis C.K. And 15 years later, this magazine identified Nate Bargatze and Nikki Glaser as burgeoning comedy titans — now, they are two of the top-selling stand-ups in the world. Over the years, Wanda Sykes, Fred Armisen, Dane Cook and Michael Che have been named Comics to Watch, as well as more recent breakouts Ayo Edebiri, Hannah Einbinder, Caleb Hearon and Julio Torres.

	The comedy industry is bigger than ever in 2026, and this year’s list represents the bold breadth of those currently making us laugh, from slacker-provocateur talk show host Adam Friedland to the musical satirist Kyle Gordon, who has been dubbed the “Millennial ‘Weird Al.’” Some stand-ups are straddling the stage and the small screen, like “Overcompensating” star Wally Baram, while others like Lucas Zelnick have built huge online followings off viral crowd-work clips. 

	Read on to see the full lineup of Variety’s 10 Comics to Watch for 2026, plus the more veteran comics endorsing them, from Glaser and Hasan Minhaj to Tim Robinson.

	You can also see the comedians perform live at a New York Comedy Festival showcase on Nov. 12, taking place at the Hard Rock Hotel in Times Square. More information, including how to buy tickets, can be found on the New York Comedy Festival website.


			
			
	Wally Baram
			
										
					Image Credit: Sami Drasin				
					
				

	Wally Baram! Wallifer Aniston, as I call her on set of “Overcompensating” at 3 a.m. on a soundstage in Toronto! I met Wally for the first time on Zoom when I was interviewing writers for “Overcompensating.” I am not being dramatic when I say it felt like fate. She entered the Zoom and I thought, “That’s Carmen.” She was exactly what I wanted for the role. But what I didn’t know was that she would be more funny, brilliant, creative, and sparkly than anything I could have dreamed of. She was vulnerable and deeply honest for the entire hour we chatted. I wanted to tell her my life story (which we would eventually act out on the aforementioned soundstage in Toronto) and felt like I knew her forever. EVERYONE who encounters her feels this way. At the end of the Zoom, I noticed that something moved in the background. I said, “Oh, do you have a dog?” to which she replied, with no ceremony, “No, that’s my pet boa constrictor named Jersey Mike.” I was in love. After the meeting, I devoured her stand-up and devastatingly funny script and hired her for the writer’s room immediately. I knew full well that she was going to get the role of Carmen when we opened auditions. I am forever lucky that I get to make a show with her by my side, and I will forever be in the front row of anything she does with Jersey Mike around my neck. — Benito Skinner

	My job before comedian was… A ball python snake breeder (in my defense, I was a teenager in college).

	The hardest I bombed was… Opening for Jeff Garlin in the Improv Lab when I was 20; I earnestly asked to start over.

	My pre-show ritual includes… I text my mom to tell her I love her before I go onstage … every single time. Is that embarrassing or what?

		
			
			
	Olivia Carter
			
										
					Image Credit: John Cafaro				
					
				

	When I discovered Olivia Carter’s clips on Instagram I had the same feeling I felt back in 2002 when I first discovered Sarah Silverman: here was a comic who was just for me. That’s not to say that she’s not for everyone else, but there was something about her dry wit, precise joke writing, and fearless delivery that made me feel like “not only do I want to consume everything she does forever and ever, but I also kind of want to be her.”

	The thing that astounds me about Olivia is that she knows exactly who she is on stage even though she’s just six years in. It’s said that it takes ten years for a comic to “find their voice” on stage, but when you watch Olivia, I’m almost certain she never had to search for it. Her material is jarring and biting, but rarely offensive because her delivery is so self-assured. Sure, her jokes might make you uncomfortable, but that’s your problem, because Olivia is right at home in the tension.

	When I guest judged the roast episode of Netflix’s “Funny AF,” I watched Olivia deliver incredibly well-written jokes about subject matter that I know she had been told by higher-ups to steer away from. I couldn’t believe the tenacity it took for her to break the “rules” on a show she was trying to win just so she could tell the best jokes possible, and more importantly: the truth. This is the moment I knew that Olivia wasn’t just a comic to watch, but the kind of comic we should all aspire to be. — Nikki Glaser

	The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A women’s prison. I made fun of the security guard and got a standing ovation. Crushed so hard they arrested me.

	The best advice a comic gave me was… “Get sleep if you can.”

	My favorite thing about comedy is… People love to tell you there are rules, but actually there are no rules.

		
			
			
	Aaron Chen
			
										
					Image Credit: Jordan Ashleigh				
					
				

	Do yourself a favor and watch a clip of Aaron Chen at the 2019 Melbourne Comedy Festival. That’s how I first got introduced to him. His mullet, every single word choice and his quiet, calm but confident delivery had me dead. My favorite joke from one of his YouTube specials is: “When people say let’s meet for a coffee, what I’m hearing is let’s go do a poo poo.” His comedy is silly but smart, weird and completely unpredictable. He’s truly one of the most exciting new voices in stand-up, and I cannot wait to see what he does next. — Ali Wong

	The hardest I bombed was… At a private club for wealthy elites. I saw some things I should not have seen. It was hard to get laughs as people were more interested in some disturbed rituals.

	The one thing I’d never joke about is… The ethnic and political tensions of Singapore in the 1960s.

	My parents think I… Don’t give a damn what anyone even says and they are correct.

	The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… The microphone is not actually on; it’s an optical illusion.

		
			
			
	Adam Friedland
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Adam Friedland				
					
				

	Who the hell is Adam Friedland? I didn’t know. My manager says he’d like me to do his podcast, and as one who doesn’t say “no” to anything, I agree. He says he wants this show to be like “The Dick Cavett Show.” It’s nothing like the “Cavett Show.” We talk a lot, make each other laugh. I throw crap at him. He throws it back. We have a great time. He has me read a ridiculous three-page script and then we talk about Nazis. Then I leave. I had a great time. He’s funny, likeable, smart, and we really get along. A few weeks later, my son calls me from college. “Dad, how do you know Adam Friedland?” I don’t. “I heard you on his show. That guy is hilarious.” I walk down the streets. One kid after another says, “You were great on Adam Friedland’s show.” And yet, I still ask: Who the hell is Adam Friedland? — Richard Kind

	The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A women’s rally six months into comedy.

	My job before comedian was… Paralegal, my true passion.

	The strangest fan interaction I’ve ever had was… An old man asked for a picture thinking I was Sarah Sherman from “Saturday Night Live.”

	My favorite thing about comedy is… That it’s not important.

		
			
			
	Kyle Gordon
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Kyle Gordon				
					
				

	The first time I heard Kyle Gordon shout, “If you want parties to be making, have some noise” in his European foam-bar anthem “Planet of the Bass,” I felt like Salieri reading the sheet music for Sonata for Woodwinds in “Amadeus.” What a cruel trick, that God had given me the power to recognize when someone as bonkers as Kyle Gordon would come along. Kyle’s albums are entitled: “Kyle Gordon is Everywhere,” “Kyle Gordon is Great” and “Kyle Gordon is Wonderful.” All of these statements are true, but Kyle Gordon is also bonkers. Kyle Gordon is crushing it in a new arena of song comedy, a genre that has been pretty upbeat for the past hundred years. While Kyle has some upbeat comedy songs (“Selekta,” “Myrtle Beach,” “Mr. Jambo”) he’s also written some of the darkest comedy songs in years: “Crawl to Me,” “If You Break Up With Me,” “I’m a Whore.” Kyle asked me if I’d like to be in the video for his hit “Irish Drinking Song.” I said, “Of course, Kyle!” Then I listened to the lyrics. A hilarious song, yes, but I knew I could never be in a video with almost any of those words in it. But Kyle wasn’t worried; that’s what makes his stuff so special — Kyle doesn’t worry, he commits. Kyle is breaking new ground in song comedy all the time. He’s a force of nature, and if it were perfectly accurate, Kyle’s next album would be called: “Kyle Gordon is Unafraid.” — Thomas Lennon

	The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… Comedy isn’t funny because it’s true. It’s funny because it feels true, whether it’s actually true or not.

	The strangest fan interaction I’ve ever had was… I signed a Ziploc bag filled with a fan’s mother’s ashes.

	The weirdest thing I’ve ever done for a laugh is… Got naked and ran on the subway tracks.

		
			
			
	Shapel Lacey
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Jim McCambridge				
					
				

	Shapel Lacey? You mean the kindest man in comedy? Please hold while I gush about my baby. *Cracks knuckles* Believe me when I tell you Shapel is the type of comic who has the audience by the balls within five words or less. There’s a rawness to his delivery that feels effortlessly personal and refreshingly candid. While watching him perform, you’re sure to find yourself completely immersed in his story. And let me add: It’s one hell of a story. What makes Shapel a star (yeah, I said it) is that he isn’t trying to fit a familiar comedic mold. He’s developing a style that’s distinctly his own. Also… you haven’t lived until you’ve had a 1 a.m. post-show recap with Shapel Lacey at Swingers Diner. Many have applied; few have received the invite. — Joe Dombrowski

	My pre-show ritual includes… Watching skateboarding or cheerleading videos on YouTube.

	The hardest I bombed was… My fourth time doing stand-up ever, at a dance club while the DJ was taking a break.

	My favorite thing about comedy is… Being able to laugh at the things that used to make me sad.

		
			
			
	Eilise Patton
			
										
					Image Credit: Emily Pinto				
					
				

	I am a massive fan of Eilise’s work. She makes me excited and hopeful for the future of comedy. Her ideas and characters feel so inspired and brand new. — Tim Robinson

	The last thing that made me laugh was… I was visiting my mother and she heard a noise outside, and I saw her type into ChatGPT: “What was that boom?”

	The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… On a Zoom during COVID for a shipping company. Everyone had their camera and mics off.

	The title of my memoir will be… “Eilise on Life” (like “A Lease on Life”!), but now I’m sure some bitch with the normal spelling of Elise will take it.

	The one thing I’d never joke about is… No such thing!

	The most important thing on my rider is… A Celsius. Must consume for energy as well as ritual. Not sponsored just deeply superstitious.

	The best advice from a comic is… Steve Martin’s “Never show doubt” has been my North Star forever. Just being fearless and fully going for it every time.

		
			
			
	Usama Siddiquee
			
										
					Image Credit: Phil Provencio				
					
				

	Usama Siddiquee is a true comic’s comic, grinding, hustling and building an undeniable act for years. I’ve known Usama for nearly a decade, and I’ve watched him work his way up from open mics to the biggest stages. When Kevin Hart crowned him live on stage at the Village Underground during his “Funny AF” taping, it may have appeared to be kismet, or a “lucky night” but it wasn’t. It’s what so many comics have known for years — Usama is undeniable, and he’s here to stay.

	He’s got it all. The charisma, charm, the smile, the act outs, the hair. My God, the waves in the hair. Look, I want him to get married, but he told me he’s married to the game. (I still don’t know what that means.)

	During the finale taping of Kevin Hart’s “Funny AF,” I remember seeing videos of the entire theater chanting his name before he even hit the stage. It made me emotional. Because he’s not a burgeoning “Comic to Watch” — he’s arrived, and we can’t stop saying his name. — Hasan Minhaj

	The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A strip club that was named Strip Club.

	The heckle I still think about is… I was killing on stage when out of nowhere an old Irish lady in the crowd told me to “get over myself. Enough is enough.” Almost quit comedy that day.

	The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… How long it takes to get good. Whatever time you think it is, it’s double that.

		
			
			
	Josh Ocean Thomas
			
										
					Image Credit: Kinda Arzon				
					
				

	I met Josh in Chicago at a Don’t Tell Comedy in some dingy dive bar, after which he would not stop trying to be my friend. He is so nice to a point where it’s suspicious, and I have to ask myself, “Is this guy for real?” Aside from being a decent human, Josh kills every time he steps on stage and offers a respite from the standard comedy you might be used to. I truly believe Josh has everything it takes to be one of the top performing comics of all time, and I say that emphatically. — Morgan Jay

	My job before becoming a comedian was… A Kayak & Snorkel Tour Guide at La Jolla Kayak in San Diego.

	The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… That all comedians are miserable people.

	My favorite thing about comedy is… Meeting other comedians who, despite being strangers and coming from completely different walks of life, share one of the most important parts of life with me. I also just love getting to do it.

	The best advice a comic gave me was… “Be kind, stay funny, and you’ll be all right” – Conan O’Brien, when I met him at 14 years old at Comic Con San Diego.

		
			
			
	Lucas Zelnick
			
										
					Image Credit: Dev Bowman				
					
				

	I think what’s been most impressive about watching Lucas’ rise is him taking on subjects that are unique to him and historically not funny at all. Most comics would avoid talking about coming from money or their mom dating Epstein (when she was an adult!). Lucas leans into it and it’s hilarious and my favorite material of his. It’s always cool to see comics get more honest as the stakes get higher and the rooms get bigger. Hollywood should call him soon before his dad makes him run the diamond mines in Botswana. — Andrew Schulz

	The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A church (I’m Jewish).

	The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… You can be edgy as long as you’re not mean-spirited.

	The strangest fan interaction I’ve ever had was… A fan let me write “I watched Lucas Zelnick bomb” on their arm and then got it tattooed.

	My favorite thing about comedy is… You can say exactly what you think and everyone acts like you’re kidding.

		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

            Blake Lively's bespoke booze beverage business is slowly shutting down following her legal battle with Justin Baldoni ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Blake launched her non-alcoholic drink line, Betty Buzz, in 2021. She expanded into alcoholic drinks with Betty Booze in 2023 ... despite admitting she doesn’t enjoy drinking alcohol.
      
    
          Waiting for your permission to load TikTok Post.
      
    
            According to trademark records reviewed by TMZ, Blake's company has filed several trademark applications since its launch. Betty Booze and Betty Buzz's trademarks are still active, but multiple others related to the company have been abandoned.
      

            The abandoned trademark applications include marks for beer-based products, non-alcoholic carbonated beverages and other products.
      
    
            Betty Buzz hasn't posted on Instagram since April 5 ... while Betty Booze hasn't posted since September 28 ... despite being very active for years. Whole Foods was known to carry the non-alcoholic line, and Total Wine carried the alcoholic products.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Blake hasn't exactly been keeping a low profile since her legal drama ended ... she was photographed Tuesday night at the Brent Neale Wrap It Up Capsule Collection event in New York City.

            Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony appear to have hashed out a settlement in their divorce ... TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            According to court records obtained by TMZ, the NBA legend and entertainer informed the court this week of the deal. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The terms of the agreement are confidential. The judge has yet to sign off.
      

            As TMZ first reported, La La filed for divorce in 2021, citing irreconcilable differences.
      
    
            The exes broke up in 2017 after 7 years of marriage ... amid rumors Melo cheated on her. They tried to work things out, but ultimately divorced.
      
    
            At the time the divorce was filed, sources told TMZ the exes had been split for a while but were still friends. Sources said the split wasn’t nasty. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The divorce was finalized after La La and Carmelo's 19-year-old son Kiyan became an adult ... making child support a moot issue. 
      
    
            Kiyan just started his college basketball career ... he's a sophomore at Syracuse University, where Melo played and won a National Championship back in the day.

title: Donald Trump Jr. Heckled at Emory Law School After Midterms, 'Country Has Rebuked You'
description:
Donald Trump Jr.
                          'The Country Has Rebuked You!!!'
body:
Donald Trump Jr.
                          'The Country Has Rebuked You!!!'
                          Heckled On College Campus
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 4, 2026
                            11:20 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 4, 2026
                                12:48 PM PST
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Here's Donald Trump Jr. getting an earful after a fireside chat at a high-ranking law school ... with students heckling him over the midterms and telling him voters are turning on his father.
      
    
            TMZ obtained video from Don Jr.'s Wednesday visit to the law school at Emory University in Atlanta ... and hecklers are shouting at the president's son, "The country has rebuked you!!!"
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A source tells TMZ ... Don Jr. was there to support his business partner Omeed Malik -- who was having his name put on a building at Emory's law school and celebrated with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at his alma mater.
      

            Apparently, students weren't told beforehand that Don Jr. -- who brought the Secret Service along with him to the campus -- was coming to the event.
      
    
            Don Jr. and Omeed are part of the same venture capital firm and are good buddies.
      
    
            Sources close to Omeed tell TMZ ... Don Jr. was with Omeed for four hours at Emory, and towards the end there was a fireside chat with about 100 students. We're told four students stood up during the chat and started yelling about fascism. It's unclear if they were law students.
      
    
            Our sources say the student protestors were escorted out of the auditorium, but continued yelling from outside. The video picks up as Don Jr. and Omeed are leaving, and we're told they knew they were being filmed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Omeed flips the protesters the bird in the video ... and we're told he wanted to make a point that they were being disrespectful.
      
    
            Our sources say the hecklers didn't ruin Omeed and Don Jr.'s day ... things went smoothly until the end of their visit, when word spread that Trump's son was on campus.
      
    
            The Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the midterms as voters sent a clear message to Trump and the GOP ... and these hecklers sent Don Jr. a clear message too.
